messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Musician
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 45

He is 50, a South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life making a living as a musician. For years, his life has been organized around sound: late-night sets in small venues, wedding gigs on weekends, teaching a few private students during the day, and long hours alone arranging music at home. After his divorce, he tells the story as if his life became quieter in some ways and more exposed in others. He lives alone, keeps odd hours, and is used to being watched in the ordinary way performers are watched. What he was not prepared for was how that attention could harden into something invasive and relentless.

It begins, he says, with a woman who starts coming regularly to his performances. At first she seems like any enthusiastic audience member. She requests the same songs, waits after shows to compliment him, brings small gifts he is too polite to refuse. He remembers feeling mildly uncomfortable but also embarrassed by his own discomfort. As a musician, he depends on people liking him. He tells himself not to be arrogant, not to overreact. When she begins messaging him repeatedly on social media, he tries to respond politely and briefly. Soon the messages multiply. If he does not answer, she sends more. She writes as if they have a private bond, referring to things he has said on stage and interpreting song lyrics as messages meant specifically for her.

Over the next months, the contact spreads into his daily life. She appears outside venues where he has not publicly posted he will be playing. She waits by his car. Once, he sees her across the street from the apartment where he teaches lessons. Another time, he opens his front door in the morning and finds flowers and a note using familiar, intimate language that makes his stomach drop. He changes his route home after gigs, starts checking mirrors while driving, starts pausing before entering his building. He laughs about it at first with musician friends, trying to make it into a strange occupational hazard, but the laughter is tight. Inside, he feels hunted.

The moment he describes as the turning point happens after a late performance. He notices her near the exit and slips out through a side door, hoping to avoid a scene. When he reaches his car, she is already there. She is crying, then accusing, then pleading, standing close enough that he can smell her perfume and feel himself backing into the door. She tells him he cannot keep ignoring what they have. He says he remembers his hands shaking so badly he drops his keys. He is less focused on what she says than on the shock that she knows which car is his, that she has anticipated his movements. He gets in, locks the doors, and drives away, but for the entire trip home he is convinced she is behind him. Even now, recounting it, he rubs his palms on his thighs as if drying sweat.

After that night, his world narrows. He files reports, blocks accounts, changes phone numbers, tells venues not to share his schedule. None of it makes him feel safe. Instead he becomes preoccupied with what he might have missed, what information about him is still available, how easily a stranger can assemble a map of his life. He stops posting performances online. He turns down gigs if the venue seems too open or if parking is poorly lit. His income drops, which humiliates him. Music had always been where he felt most competent, most himself. Now the stage lights make him feel visible in the wrong way. In the middle of songs, his eyes move to the door. If someone stands in the back too long, he loses his place for a beat. He says he has become a musician who cannot stop scanning the room.

Sleep becomes thin and unreliable. He lies down exhausted but stays alert to hallway sounds, footsteps, a car slowing outside. When he does sleep, he wakes abruptly, heart pounding, unsure whether he heard knocking or dreamed it. Some mornings he finds himself already tense before he is fully awake. He keeps curtains closed. He checks locks repeatedly, then feels foolish, then checks again. On days when he has students coming, he watches from the window to make sure it is really them. Unexpected messages, even harmless ones, create a spike of panic before he can think.

He also speaks about the shame. He is a middle-aged man, physically larger than the person who stalked him, and he believes other people expect him to brush it off. He has heard jokes when men talk about unwanted attention from women. For a long time he minimizes what happened, even to himself. But in quieter moments he notices how much his life has changed. He sees it in the way he sits in restaurants facing the entrance, in the way he avoids familiar neighborhoods where she once appeared, in the stack of unopened fan messages he cannot bring himself to read. He misses the part of performing that used to feel generous and connecting. Now, even when a set goes well, he feels relief more than joy when it is over.

In the present, he is still working, still teaching, still taking gigs selectively, but with a guardedness that seems to cost him. He describes himself as always measuring risk. He wants to be absorbed in rhythm and melody again, to lose track of himself inside the music, but instead he keeps returning to the same vigilant question: who is watching, and what do they want from me?
